Objective:
A wiki is a collaboratively edited website or hypertext publication that users can create, modify, and link directly through a web browser. The term comes from the Hawaiian word wiki ("quick"), originating with Ward Cunningham's 1995 site WikiWikiWeb.

Key Features & Uses

• Collaborative editing: Multiple contributors can add or revise content and track version history.
• Simple formatting: Many wikis use lightweight markup or simple syntax instead of complex HTML, making quick updates easy.
• Public & internal use: Wikis power open public resources as well as private company or team knowledge hubs.

Usage Examples

• Public reference & media: Wiki concepts are most famously used by Wikipedia, alongside sister projects like Wiktionary and Wikimedia Commons, as well as fandom or how-to sites.
• Workplace documentation: Teams use internal wikis to store onboarding guides, meeting notes, project plans, and company policies.

Related Terms & Synonyms

• Collaborative knowledge base (closely related, though traditional knowledge bases often restrict editing to specific roles)
• Team documentation / internal handbook (in workplace contexts)
• Living document / collaborative hypertext (descriptive equivalents)
